extracted.intended_audience: Investigators and applicants submitting NIH grant applications (R01, R21, R35, K99, K08, F32, F31, R15, R56), especially ESIs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice and procedural standards for preparing, submitting, and managing NIH grant applications (including resubmissions, JIT, overlap issues, NOSIs, study section assignment, and ESI rules). Geared toward how to increase fundability and handle post-review steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wait for the summary statement before contacting PO
rubrics_metrics.description: When you get your summary statement, you can get in touch with your PO for next steps (which could include advice to submit again for insurance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program Officers need the summary statement to see the specific concerns raised; email them first (they prefer email to unscheduled calls) and then schedule a phone/Zoom if needed. The PO won't know firm funding likelihood until after the federal budget is signed (often 6–8 weeks after).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use JIT to check for overlap and expect discussion then
rubrics_metrics.description: When you submit JIT for an award, they will check for overlap with other active or pending support, and this is when discussions about overlap happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to discuss each application and propose modifications needed to eliminate budgetary and scientific overlap. In JIT Other Support explicitly discuss partial overlap and state that if both projects are funded, scope and budget will be adjusted in conjunction with NIH staff to eliminate overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: If two ICs consider overlapping projects, be prepared to choose or revise
rubrics_metrics.description: If two applications are too similar for both to be funded as independent projects, you may need to choose one or substantially modify one to eliminate overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each IC likes the science they won't discount an application because overlap needs resolution, but the projects must be sufficiently different in aims, goals, outcomes, approach, etc., to stand alone after overlap is removed. If not, you may be asked to pick one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding order determines overlap resolution (first funder has priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whichever IC processes an award first would fund the full amount, and the second award would be cut to remove overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If negotiations are simultaneous, some mechanisms (e.g., R35) may be less flexible. Consider institutional caps (e.g., NIGMS cap for well-funded investigators) in planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contacting the PO: email first, then meeting; PO's advice is authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact your PO after receiving the summary statement via email first; they may schedule a call and will advise whether to resubmit or prepare rebuttals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POs are busy and prefer email. Trust PO judgments about fundability more than colleagues' optimism; colleagues may try to comfort you, but POs give practical funding likelihood and next-step advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: POs won't know funding likelihood until the budget is set
rubrics_metrics.description: POs generally will not have funding information until after the federal budget is signed into law (often creating a 6–8 week delay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect uncertainty during continuing resolutions; POs may recommend you resubmit 'for insurance' because funding decisions are delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask PO whether to resubmit and address summary concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have your summary statement, ask your PO whether you should submit again (even just for insurance), and consider how to respond to concerns raised in the Summary of Discussion paragraph(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POs can advise whether an A1 or a new A0 is appropriate. Use the summary statement to guide revisions and to craft a targeted rebuttal or revised aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus rebuttals on the Summary of Discussion paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a short rebuttal/response for the PO that focuses on the weaknesses described in the Summary of Discussion paragraph, since those were discussed by the panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep rebuttal to a page or two (unless PO requests otherwise). Explain how you will address the panel-discussed weaknesses, summarize new data/publications since submission, and include a concise 'Overall Impact' closing paragraph/sentence if missing from the aims page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address only panel-discussed issues in PO rebuttals (not every individual critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not need to address all individual reviewer critiques in the PO rebuttal—focus on those noted in the Summary of Discussion (the issues discussed by the panel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This keeps the rebuttal concise and targeted to what influenced the panel; save broader addressing of other critiques for the next submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a clear Overall Impact statement on Aims page
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an 'Overall Impact' closing paragraph or sentence on your Aims page to make it easy for reviewers to see the significance and translation of your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear closing helps reviewers write their reviews and ensures the importance to the field and public health is explicit; add this both in the rebuttal and in future submissions if absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile is not the same as success probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentile doesn’t equal success rate; a borderline percentile may have a wide range of funding chance depending on IC practices and PO advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the PO’s judgement of funding likelihood rather than colleagues' anecdotal impressions. A borderline score could have ~10–25% chance depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI status and payline rules — reviewed vs award-time handling
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH policy: If an ESI-eligible application is awarded and the same PD/PI has an R01 or R01-equivalent application pending review, the pending application will be reviewed as an ESI-eligible application. However, the status of the pending application will be updated after release of the Summary Statement to acknowledge the application is no longer ESI-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You effectively get the ESI consideration for only one award; if an award is made first, subsequent pending applications will lose ESI eligibility at the Summary Statement stage. Do not include established PIs as MPIs on your ESI-eligible application — mixed MPI applications lose ESI benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never include an established PI as an MPI on ESI-eligible applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Including an established PI as an MPI on an ESI-eligible application forfeits ESI status for that application (and may affect future applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need expertise, list established investigators as co-investigators, collaborators, or key personnel rather than MPIs to preserve ESI eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section assignment: suggest SRG but justify with science
rubrics_metrics.description: You will submit to the FOA with which a NOSI is linked; for the parent announcement you can suggest an SRG on the PHS assignment request form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective evidence (Matchmaker, CSR ART, PO advice) to justify SRG requests. SROs need robust, objective reasons to move assignments; requests must be based on science, not dislike of particular reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO ensures reviewers are independent and won't consider other applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The SRO makes sure related applications have different reviewers and that discussion will not refer to other applications; each application is reviewed on its own merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You generally do not need to worry about multiple submissions to the same study section being unfairly compared, but ICs decide on funding of multiple grants to one investigator in the same cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: NOSI handling: submit to linked FOA; no automatic special payline
rubrics_metrics.description: You will submit your application to the FOA with which the NOSI is linked; the FOA determines the locus of review. There is no special payline for NOSIs generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some NOSIs indicate special funding consideration or set-asides; many simply advertise priority topics and may be funded on top of FOA awards. Check the NOSI for extra instructions or funding language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reusing A1 experiments in other proposals is allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: You can rework non-overlapping new experiments proposed in an A1 into a new proposal for NIH or NSF (but not submit identical proposals to both agencies simultaneously).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk with program directors at agencies to see who is more interested and which FOAs fit. Ensure appropriate redaction or framing if some material overlaps with a funded A0.

rubrics_metrics.name: R15 eligibility is based on submitting unit; conversion to R01 is possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility for R15 is based on the submitting unit (school); if your school is no longer eligible you cannot resubmit R15 from that school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your unit loses eligibility, discuss with the PO about converting the project to an R01-level submission; the R01 would be a new submission and not formally related to the R15.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can submit another application while one is pending under conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Summary Statement has been released then you can submit the exact same application or a different one; if science is very different you might have been able to submit a different one even before SS release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting a new application generally does not automatically withdraw a pending application, but check specific FOA rules and discuss timing with your PO to avoid conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending/completed statuses: 'Pending' plus JIT is a good signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending status on Commons is a positive signal if it is accompanied by a JIT request; pending could also be administrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have not received a personal JIT request but see Pending, ask your GMS or PO for guidance about whether you should submit JIT information and why your status is listed as Pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use RePORTER Matchmaker and CSR ART to justify SRG requests
rubrics_metrics.description: To request a different study section, cite high ranking in RePORTER Matchmaker and the CSR Assisted Referral Tool (ART) as justification, and ask the PO for recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document objective evidence that your science fits better in another SRG to increase chances SRO will change assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: When revising, ensure you consider current state of the science (not just tweak)
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior submissions show recurring concerns (e.g., about significance), fundamental changes may be needed rather than incremental tweaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step back from the summary statement to make substantive changes when appropriate—ensure aims remain compelling given recent publications/data and the field's evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be strategic when writing for clinical vs engineering SRGs
rubrics_metrics.description: If your application sits at the clinical-translation/informatics interface and is being reviewed by engineering-heavy SRGs, consider targeting clinical SRGs or rewording aims to highlight clinical impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain translational utility and data analysis details clearly. If the SRG mix is suboptimal, consult your PO and use Matchmaker/ART/SRG requests to try to place the application where reviewers will appreciate the clinical application.
